items.item: shuffleTracking.enabled keeps alive executors holding shuffle data for active jobs, without an external shuffle service
shuffleTracking.timeout defaults to infinity
decommission.enabled tries to shut an executor down gracefully, migrating RDD and shuffle blocks to a remote executor
storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled requires a migratable shuffle resolver (sort-based shuffle)

items.item: the product's current name, replacing Dataproc on Compute Engine and Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark
Spark on GKE creates node pools inside an existing GKE cluster instead of separate master/worker VMs
Kueue manages quotas and decides when a job is admitted, waits, or is preempted

on Kubernetes the driver is the cluster manager for the lifetime of one application — there is no standing cluster manager that pre-exists the submission the way YARN or a Spark standalone master does, which is why the OwnerReference is the only cleanup mechanism and not a convenience

at.deep: The driver is the cluster manager, briefly

items.item: client mode (driver outside a pod, or in a pod without its name set correctly) does not get automatic executor cleanup via OwnerReference at all — the docs' own warning about setting it to the wrong pod is a narrower case of the same gap

at.step: The tie that cleans up executors

items.item: shuffleTracking's infinite default timeout is a deliberate design choice stated in the docs themselves (reliance on shuffle garbage collection, not a timer), not an oversight — lowering it trades resource usage against the risk of recomputing data that turns out still to be needed

at.deep: Garbage collection as a cleanup mechanism, on purpose

items.item: decommission's block migration only helps if it finishes before the node is actually reclaimed — a migration interrupted partway through still loses whatever wasn't migrated yet, so decommissioning is a race against the interruption warning, not an unconditional guarantee

the Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator and the Kubeflow Spark Operator are both active, separately maintained projects with different custom-resource APIs (spark.apache.org vs. sparkoperator.k8s.io) — neither supersedes the other, and a team choosing between them is choosing a dependency, not a successor

Google's GKE Spark offering has been renamed at least twice (Dataproc on Compute Engine / Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark to Managed Service for Apache Spark), so older documentation and tutorials referencing 'Dataproc on GKE' describe the same current product under its old name

at.out: a naming-history detail below this topic's scope; named for a learner who finds older material

items.item: pod templates are unmarshalled by Spark without validation — the Kubernetes API server is what actually rejects an invalid template, which can surface as a cryptic scheduling failure rather than an upfront Spark error

at.out: an operational debugging detail below this topic's scope

items.item: EMR on EKS's naming convention ('emr-containers' as the API/CLI prefix) is a historical artifact of how the service was introduced, separate from the EMR-on-EC2 product line's own naming

at.out: an AWS-specific naming detail below this topic's scope

items.item: Kueue's partial-admission and dynamic-reclaim mechanisms let a job run with reduced parallelism under tight quota and release capacity incrementally as pods complete, which is the specific feature that resolves the two-jobs gang-scheduling deadlock this chapter's skipped syllabus topic names

block migration during decommissioning specifically requires a migratable shuffle resolver (sort-based shuffle, the Spark default) — a custom or legacy hash-based shuffle implementation would not support the same graceful migration path
